Pinning dependencies with lockfiles

By Dana Field · June 2, 2025

Every build that resolves version ranges at install time is a build that can change without a single line of your code changing. A lockfile records the exact versions that were resolved, together with integrity hashes, so that the next install reproduces the same tree on every machine and in continuous integration.

This post walks through how lockfiles work in three package managers, what the integrity field protects against, and how to keep the file healthy when several people update dependencies at once. The short version is that the lockfile belongs in version control and should be updated deliberately.

What a lockfile records

For each package the lockfile stores the resolved version, the registry URL it came from and a hash of the tarball. When the hash of a downloaded tarball does not match, the install fails instead of silently running different code. See the integrity hashes explainer and the format reference for details.

Updating safely

  1. Run the update command on a branch, never on the main branch directly.
  2. Review the lockfile diff: unexpected new packages deserve a second look.
  3. Let continuous integration install from the lockfile with the frozen flag.

In CI, install with the frozen option so a stale lockfile fails the build:

pnpm install --frozen-lockfile
npm ci
ManagerLockfile
npmpackage-lock.json
pnpmpnpm-lock.yaml

Treat the lockfile like any other source file: review it, keep it small by pruning unused dependencies, and regenerate it only when you mean to.
